note:
Or “slave of God,” one who is owned by and who serves God (Rom. 1:1; Phil. 1:1).

**apostle of Jesus Christ.** One sent out as an eyewitness of the resurrected Christ and as His official representative (2 Cor. 1:1 note; 1 Tim. 1:1 note).

**for the sake of the faith ... godliness.** The goal of Paul’s apostleship is faith in Christ, which is grounded in knowledge and leads to godly living on the part of God’s elect (see Rom. 1:5). Paul does not simply desire to convey information, but to see God’s people grow in godliness through a believing reception of the truth he proclaims. Paul will note that the appearing of God’s grace in Christ trains believers to renounce evil passions and live godly lives (2:11, 12), devoted to good works (3:4–8).

**God’s elect.** Those whom God has chosen to believe in Christ (cf. John 15:16; 1 Cor. 1:26–31; 2 Tim. 2:10).

The blessings secured by Christ that believers experience in part presently, and in full at Christ’s return (1 Tim. 1:1, 16 note; 2 Tim. 1:1).

**who never lies.** An affirmation of the complete trustworthiness of God (Num. 23:19). His Word (v. 3) is therefore entirely trustworthy.

**promised before the ages began.** Affirmation of the eternal nature of the divine decree of redemption through Christ (2 Tim. 1:9).
As author of the covenant of grace, God is Savior (2:10; 3:4; 1 Tim. 1:1; 2:3; 4:10).

Titus was a Gentile believer (Gal. 2:1–3). If the epistle to the Galatians was written before the council recorded in Acts 15 (see Introduction to Galatians: Date and Occasion), his conversion was the fruit of Barnabas’s and Paul’s early ministry in Antioch of Syria (Acts 11:19–30). While ministering in Ephesus, Paul sent Titus on a delicate mission to Corinth, bearing a letter of rebuke that Paul had composed in tears to seek reconciliation with that church (2 Cor. 2:1–4, 13; 7:6–9). Paul trusted Titus to coordinate the collection from Gentile churches for relief of believers in Judea (2 Cor. 8:6, 16, 23; 12:18). Although Paul addresses this letter specifically to Titus, he intends for it to be read to the whole church (3:15 note).

**true child.** Lit. “legitimate son” (1 Tim. 1:2). This probably indicates that Titus was one of Paul’s converts.

**Grace and peace.** See note on 1 Tim. 1:2. For Paul, these two blessings summarize the blessings that Christ has secured for His people.

**Christ Jesus our Savior.** As mediator of the covenant of grace, Christ is Savior (2:13; 3:6; 2 Tim. 1:10). Paul uses the title “Savior” interchangeably for both God and Christ throughout this letter (v. 3 note), reflecting the apostle’s belief in the deity of Christ (2:13).

Paul moves into the body of the letter. His intention is to instruct Titus regarding how to act as Paul’s representative on Crete (Introduction: Date and Occasion). He begins by discussing church organization.

**1:5 I left you in Crete.** An island in the eastern Mediterranean, south of the Aegean Sea. The ship on which Paul was transported to Rome (in response to his appeal to the emperor) put in briefly at a small harbor on Crete’s southern coast, Fair Havens (Acts 27:7–12). It is unlikely, however, that this brief stopover is the background of this epistle, for two reasons: (1) The tasks before Titus after Paul’s departure presuppose and follow up on the apostle’s evangelistic ministry on Crete. (2) As he writes, Paul is free to travel and expects to winter in Nicopolis, a city on the west coast of Greece (3:12). Paul’s and Titus’s ministry in Crete probably took place after his release from his first imprisonment in Rome (See Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**put what remained into order.** As the rest of the verse makes clear, what was left unfinished were details pertaining to the organization of the newly formed churches.

**elders.** A group of individuals charged with the spiritual oversight and leadership of a local church (Acts 14:23; 20:17; 1 Tim. 5:17). As v. 7 makes clear, Paul used the term interchangeably with “overseer.” Paul discusses the qualifications for overseers in similar terms, yet with some differences, in 1 Tim. 3:2–7. Paul intends neither list to be complete, but simply to indicate the kind of character that those who are qualified to serve as church leaders must possess.
Probably a reference to marital fidelity (1 Tim. 3:2 note).

Paul’s casual shift from “elder” to “overseer” shows that he understands the two terms as referring to the same office: “elder” suggesting one’s character (spiritually mature) and “overseer” suggesting one’s task (Acts 20:17, 28).

**God’s steward.** Stewards were slaves (see v. 1) entrusted with authority to manage their masters’ estates, and therefore accountable to their masters for the preservation and expansion of their properties (Luke 16:1–13). Paul here extends the metaphor that he applied earlier to his own apostolic ministry (1 Cor. 4:1, 2) to the responsibility of all elders (see Acts 20:28 for the same charge via the shepherding metaphor).

**greedy for gain.** A greedy desire to gain great wealth should not be the motive that drives a man into church leaders (v. 11; cf. 1 Tim. 6:5, 10). However, that does not mean church leaders are required to live in poverty, for Paul calls for remunerating certain church leaders (1 Tim. 5:17).
Or, sensible and sober-minded. The call for self-control is a major emphasis of this letter (2:2, 4–6, 12).

As in his letters to Timothy, Paul is concerned with the transmission of and commitment to sound doctrine in accordance with the gospel (1 Tim. 1:10 note).

**rebuke those who contradict.** Two tasks of the elder that are especially relevant in view of the false teachers on Crete are teaching sound doctrine (1 Tim. 3:2) and refuting that which is false (Acts 20:29, 30).

Paul’s mention of the necessity to refute false teaching leads him into a discussion of the false teachers and how Titus is to deal with them.

**1:10 those of the circumcision.** This is not a reference to Jewish Christians per se, but to those Jewish Christians who understood circumcision to be necessary for the Christian’s salvation (Acts 15:1, 5; Gal. 6:12, 13).

This may refer to the false teachers’ activity in churches meeting in private homes, thus the necessity for better organization (v. 5).

**shameful gain.** See note on v. 7.

**what they ought not to teach.** Their teaching was not in accord with “sound doctrine” (v. 9).

Paul quotes Epimenides, a sixth-century B.C. poet and religious reformer from the city of Knossos on Crete, who was known for his predictions and wisdom. Paul is not placing Epimenides on the same level as the OT prophets; he is simply appealing to the esteem in which Epimenides was held in the ancient world and confirming the accuracy of Epimenides’s observations concerning the ethical defects that were characteristic of his countrymen.
He means the false teachers (2 Tim. 2:25, 26), and probably also their followers.

Perhaps a reference to the kinds of legends about OT figures that are found in many non-canonical Jewish writings (1 Tim. 1:4; 4:7; 2 Tim. 4:4).

**commands.** These are probably related to the false teachers’ distinctive and erroneous interpretations of the Jewish law (3:9; 1 Tim. 1:7; 4:3).

verse_quote: To the pure, all things are pure.
note: The false teachers apparently prohibited the use of certain things that God permits His people to use (1 Tim. 4:3 note). For Paul’s response, see 1 Tim. 4:3–5.

The NT teaches that lacking actions consistent with a changed life renders one’s faith in Christ suspect (Matt. 7:16–20; James 2:14–16; 1 John 3:17).

**by their works.** Paul condemns not only the doctrine of the false teachers, but also their actions (2 Tim. 3:2–5). Both sound doctrine and actions in accordance with a changed life are necessary for Christians (see 1:1, 2).

Paul now turns to the kinds of things that Titus, in contrast with the false teachers, ought to teach and concludes with a meditation on the grace of God.

**2:1 sound doctrine.** The term “sound” implies that true doctrine preserves and promotes spiritual health (see 1:9). See note on 1 Tim. 1:10.

As in 1 Tim. 5:1, 2, Paul prescribes instructions to be given to various groups (older men, older women, young women, young men, and slaves) regarding the virtues and behavior that make up the fitting response for each group to the grace of the gospel.

**2:2 sober-minded.** The quality of sober-mind­ed­ness dominates Paul’s advice in this section (vv. 4–6, 12; 1:8 and note).

Older women are to exhibit the spiritual maturity appropriate to their teaching role and are also to exemplify to young women their roles as Christian wives and mothers.

**teach what is good.** Probably, as the next verse suggests, in the sense of their manner in the home.

That is, “bring them to their senses.” This is a verbal form of the adjective translated “sober-minded” (v. 2) and “self-controlled” (v. 5) throughout this section. Paul probably has in mind the kinds of problems that some of the younger widows encountered at Ephesus (1 Tim. 5:11–13).

Lit. “sober-minded” (vv. 2, 4, 6, 12; 1:8 note).

**working at home.** Or, “busy at home.” This does not forbid their employment elsewhere. Paul is concerned to prevent these women from idleness and being busybodies. Contrast the behavior of some of the younger widows at Ephesus (1 Tim. 5:13).

**submissive.** Part of being “sober-minded” is embracing the order that God has given for the home. See note on 1 Tim. 2:11.

**that the word of God may not be reviled.** Paul’s overriding concern throughout this section is that the behavior of Christians reflect positively on the gospel (vv. 8, 10; see 1 Pet. 3:1–6).

Paul gives similar counsel to Timothy (1 Tim. 4:12 note).

**good works.** One of Paul’s main themes in this letter from here on (v. 14; 3:1, 8, 14). It is primarily by the doing of good works that believers commend the gospel to non-Christians.

Paul gives instructions to slaves in Eph. 6:5–8; Col. 3:22–25; and 1 Tim. 6:1, 2. Paul does not affirm slavery as a positive good. Instead, he calls slaves and masters to live in God-honoring ways toward one another.

See notes on vv. 5, 7. Whereas Paul’s concern in vv. 5 and 8 was to forestall occasions of justifiable criticism from those outside the faith, here he motivates slaves by the positive prospect that their faithful service will display the beauty of the gospel.

These verses provide the theological basis for the practical instructions given in vv. 2–10, showing that the saving grace of God and the redemptive suffering of Jesus Christ are directed toward the purpose of the godly living and good works of God’s redeemed people.

**2:11 the grace of God.** The unmerited favor or compassion of God.

**has appeared.** That is, in the person and work of Jesus Christ (3:4, 6; cf. 2 Tim. 1:10).

**bringing salvation.** God’s purpose in extending grace to sinners is their salvation (3:4–7; cf. 2 Tim. 1:9).

**all people.** All types of people, regardless of gender, age, or social class are in view (vv. 2–10; 1 Tim. 2:1–6). See notes on 1 Tim. 2:1, 6; theological note “Definite Atonement” on p. 1875.

verse_quote: our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory.
note:
The second coming of Christ (1 Tim. 6:14; 2 Tim. 4:1, 8). See theological note “Hope” on p. 2206.

**our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.** In the Greek, this construction identifies the “Savior Jesus Christ” with “our great God.” Here Paul explicitly affirms the deity of Christ (cf. Rom. 9:5; John 1:1; 20:28).

That is, on the cross. Paul follows with two purposes of the work of Christ on the cross.

**redeem us from all lawlessness.** Paul’s first point focuses on the individual: Christ paid the price necessary to free people from their sins (Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45; 1 Tim. 2:6; 1 Pet. 1:18, 19).

**purify for himself a people for his own possession.** Paul’s second point focuses on the church: Christ purifies individuals from their sins (Heb. 9:14; 1 John 1:7, 9) so that together they might constitute a people special to Him (Ex. 19:5; Ezek. 37:23; 1 Pet. 2:9). On Christ’s purifying the church, see Eph. 5:25–27.

**zealous for good works.** See note on v. 7. Far from fostering complacency, Christ’s redeeming grace even more strongly motivates believers’ grateful love, expressed in obedience (Luke 7:41–47; 1 Cor. 15:8–10; Phil. 3:7–14).

An appropriate summation of the two dimensions of Paul’s charge to Titus in vv. 2–10 and 1:10–16.

**with all authority.** That is, as Paul’s representative, and as an elder in Christ’s church.

**Let no one disregard you.** See v. 8; 1 Tim. 4:12.

Having provided instructions for specific groups, Paul now gives Titus general counsel, centered around another meditation on the grace of God, on encouraging the people to do “every good work” (v. 1).

**3:1 rulers and authorities.** On Christian submission to governing authorities, see Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17; cf. 1 Tim. 2:2.

**every good work.** The theme for this section is doing good (v. 8; 2:7 note).
This verse presents a graphic description of human depravity apart from Christ (Eph. 2:1–3; Rom. 1:28–32).

verse_quote: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared.
note: Paul ties our salvation (v. 5) to the work accomplished by Christ at His first advent. The terms “goodness” and “loving kindness” emphasize that our salvation is by grace alone.

Paul’s words in v. 3 show that from which believers have been saved.

**not because of works ... but according to his own mercy.** Salvation is by the grace of God, not by believers’ own works (v. 6; Eph. 2:8, 9; 2 Tim. 1:9).

**washing.** Spiritual cleansing, of which baptism is the sign and seal (1 Cor. 6:11; Eph. 5:26).

**of regeneration and renewal.** Both words characterize the “washing.” “Regeneration” is the new life that begins when a person comes to faith in Christ (John 3:3, 5; 1 Pet. 1:3, 23). In the outworking of salvation, regeneration actually precedes faith. We cannot see, let alone enter the kingdom of God unless He first changes our hearts (John 3:3, 5). Renewal is closely related to rebirth; it signifies the complete transformation of a person’s life that begins when one is regenerated (Rom. 12:2; 2 Cor. 5:17). See theological note “Rebirth” on p. 1857.

**of the Holy Spirit.** The Spirit applies to individuals the grace of God that is extended in Christ (John 3:5, 6). Note the Trinitarianism of vv. 4–6. God (the Father) saves us by the regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, who is poured out on us through Christ.

Declared righteous before God (Rom. 4; 5; Gal. 3; 4).

**by his grace.** Left to ourselves (vv. 3, 4), we could never stand righteous before God. The point of vv. 3–7 is that righteousness comes through God’s grace alone, and we receive it by faith alone in Christ alone (Rom. 3:21–26).

**heirs.** God’s purpose in extending His grace to sinners is not only to save them from eternal judgment, but to make them part of His family through adoption and thus heirs of His promises (Rom. 8:17; Gal. 3:29; 4:7).

See note on 1 Tim. 1:15. The expression points back to vv. 4–7.

**good works.** See note on v. 1. Once again, Paul underscores the necessary connection between professing faith in Christ and devoting one’s life to His service in obedience to His commands.

By way of contrast with the instructions he has just given, Paul returns one last time to the problem of the false teachers. Only the gospel—not false teaching—is capable of bringing the blessings and renewal of which Paul spoke in 3:1–8.

**3:9 controversies, genealogies.** A prominent characteristic of the false teachers was their contentiousness (1 Tim. 1:4; 6:4). Controversy need not be sinful, but “foolish controversies” always are. Biblical genealogies have a vital purpose, demonstrating God’s faithfulness in keeping His covenant and His promises throughout the generations, but according to the books of 1 Timothy and Titus, false teachers found ways to distort and misuse these portions of Scripture (3:9; cf. 1 Tim. 1:4).

**about the law.** The law of Moses (1:10 note; cf. 1 Tim. 1:7).

**unprofitable.** To be contrasted with doing what is good, which is “profitable” (v. 8).

Church discipline involves a series of warnings designed to call the sinning brother to repentance (Matt. 18:15–17). For certain types of sins, it is appropriate to withdraw oneself from close fellowship with the recalcitrant person while issuing a loving warning and treating the offender as a brother in Christ (2 Thess. 3:14, 15). However, for those who threaten a congregation’s unity, the process of warning leading to excommunication must be considered seriously and carefully. Nevertheless, the purpose of excommunication is ultimately restorative, as seen in 1 Cor. 5:4, 5. The hope is that the person might finally confess their sin and return to the fellowship of the church.

**division.** The false teachers had caused division in the churches (1 Tim. 6:4, 5).

Paul closes the letter with personal instructions to Titus, final greetings, and a benediction.

**3:12 Artemas.** Mentioned nowhere else in the NT, he was apparently one of Paul’s coworkers.

**Tychicus.** A coworker of Paul mentioned in Acts 20:4; Eph. 6:21; Col. 4:7; 2 Tim. 4:12.

**come to me.** Titus’s ministry on Crete was nearing its end when Paul wrote his letter to Titus (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**Nicopolis.** A city on the west coast of the Roman province of Epirus (west of Achaia, in modern-day Albania), on the Adriatic Sea.

**I have decided to ... winter there.** Paul may be in Macedonia, planning to travel southwest to the milder climate of a seaside city.

Probably the bearers of this letter. Zenas is mentioned nowhere else in the NT; he is apparently one of Paul’s coworkers. Apollos was a native of Alexandria and noted for his eloquence (Acts 18:24–26). He is best known for his ministry at Corinth (Acts 18:27–19:1; 1 Cor. 1:12; 3:4–22; 16:12).
See note on 2:7. Given Paul’s emphasis upon good works as the necessary fruit of the gospel in the lives of the redeemed, this exhortation provides a fitting conclusion to the letter.
Paul apparently intended the letter to be read to the entire church, given that the “you” is plural in Greek and that Paul adds the term “all” (cf. plural “you” in 1 Tim. 6:21; 2 Tim. 4:22).
